sections.text: ## Antiquity: Cicero's Foundational Debate

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: Cicero (*De Optimo Genere Oratorum*, 46 BCE) is the first theorist of translation in the Western tradition:

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: **The problem**: Cicero was translating Greek orators (Aeschines and Demosthenes) into Latin. He faced a choice.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: **His solution**: Translate not *verbum pro verbo* (word for word) but *sensum exprimere* (express the meaning). The goal is to preserve the force and quality of the argument, not the linguistic form.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther
History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
WORD-FOR-WORD (verbum pro verbo):
  • Translate each source word with a target word
  • Preserve grammatical structure
  • Follow source order
  Result: "an interpreter, not an orator" — mechanical,
  loses argumentative power and rhetorical force

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
SENSE-FOR-SENSE (sensum exprimere):
  • Capture the meaning, not the words
  • Use native Latin rhetoric
  • Add or subtract as Latin style demands
  Result: the Greek speeches "speak Latin" —
  readers encounter the argumentative force
  in their own rhetorical tradition

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
Cicero's self-description: "I did not think I ought
  to count them [the words] out to the reader like
  coins, but to pay them by weight, as it were."
```

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: **Why this matters**: Cicero established the dominant Western translation method for 1,500 years. He also set up the tension that has never been resolved — the formal/dynamic equivalence debate is Cicero's debate, rediscovered and elaborated in every century.

sections.text: ## Jerome: The Vulgate (382 CE)

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: Pope Damasus commissioned Jerome to produce a reliable Latin Bible — the Greek and Latin texts in circulation had too many variant readings and contradictions.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: Jerome's work (382-405 CE) resulted in the Vulgate (*vulgata editio* = "common edition"), which became the official Catholic Bible and was translated from for another thousand years.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: ### Jerome's Translation Principles

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: Jerome essentially applied Cicero's sense-for-sense method — *except* for scripture:

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: > "In translating [secular texts] I render not word-for-word, but sense-for-sense. But in the case of the Holy Scriptures, even the order of the words is a mystery." (*Letter 57 to Pammachius*)

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: This exception for scripture had enormous consequences. It made word-for-word translation seem more reverent — closer to God's intended word — and fueled the demand for literal translations of scripture across centuries.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther
History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
HEBREW almah → LATIN virgo
  Hebrew: almah = "young woman" (not necessarily virgin)
  Greek LXX: parthenos = "virgin" (stronger)
  Jerome follows LXX: virgo
  → Isaiah 7:14: "a young woman shall conceive"
     becomes "a virgin shall conceive"
  → Christological interpretation now embedded
     in the Latin text
  → Catholic theology built on Vulgate's "virgo"

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
"HAIL, FULL OF GRACE" (Luke 1:28)
  Greek: kecharitomene = "one who has been favored"
  Jerome: gratia plena = "full of grace"
  → Stronger than Greek; elevated Mary's status
  → Immaculate Conception doctrine partly grounded in
     Jerome's amplified translation

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
PENITENTIAM AGITE vs. METANOEITE
  Greek: metanoeite = "repent, change your mind"
  Jerome: paenitentiam agite = "do penance"
  → Greek suggests interior change
  → Latin suggests exterior acts of penance
  → This distinction fueled the Reformation debate
     over the sacrament of penance
  → Luther's 95 Theses begin from Erasmus's
     correct translation of metanoeite as "repent"
     (interior), not "do penance" (exterior + institutional)
```

sections.text: ## The Toledo School: Arabic to Latin (1085-1280)

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: The most consequential translation project in medieval intellectual history was largely invisible to its beneficiaries for centuries.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: **The background**: When the Western Roman Empire collapsed (5th century CE), Western Europe lost most of Greek philosophy and science. Greek texts survived in Byzantium (Greek East) and were translated into Arabic by the Abbasid caliphate (particularly at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, 8th-9th centuries). Islamic scholars (al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Avicenna, Averroes) then extensively commented on and extended these texts.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: **Toledo**: When Toledo was reconquered from Islamic rule (1085), Christian scholars encountered one of the great libraries of Islamic scholarship. The Toledo school of translators (Archbishop Raymond's patronage, ~1130-1280) translated Arabic texts into Latin — conveying Aristotle, Euclid, al-Khwarizmi, Galen, and Islamic science back to Western Europe.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther
History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
GREEK ORIGINALS
  (Aristotle, Euclid, Hippocrates, Galen)
         │
         ▼ (5th-6th c. CE)
  SYRIAC TRANSLATIONS
  (Christian scholars in Syria and Iraq)
         │
         ▼ (8th-10th c.)
  ARABIC TRANSLATIONS + EXTENSIONS
  (House of Wisdom, Baghdad;
   al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Avicenna, Averroes;
   al-Khwarizmi adds algebra)
         │
         ▼ (11th-12th c., Toledo)
  LATIN TRANSLATIONS
  (Gerard of Cremona, Adelard of Bath,
   Michael Scot, Herman the German)
         │
         ▼
  EUROPEAN UNIVERSITIES
  (Paris, Bologna, Oxford)
  Aristotle becomes "the Philosopher"
  Aquinas reconciles Aristotle with Christianity
  (Scholasticism)
  → Foundation of European medieval science
    and philosophy

sections.text:
WITHOUT TOLEDO: The Scientific Revolution is
  delayed by generations. Algebra (al-Khwarizmi)
  reaches Europe via this chain. "Algorithm" is
  Latinization of "al-Khwarizmi."

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
Key translators:
- **Gerard of Cremona** (1114-1187): Translated ~80 works from Arabic to Latin, including Ptolemy's *Almagest*, Avicenna's *Canon of Medicine*, al-Khwarizmi's *Algebra*
- **Adelard of Bath**: Translated Euclid's *Elements* from Arabic, introducing rigorous geometric proof to Western Europe
- **Herman the German**: Translated Aristotle's *Poetics*, *Rhetoric*, *Nicomachean Ethics*

sections.text: ## Luther's German Bible (1522)

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: Martin Luther's translation of the New Testament (September 1522) is one of the most consequential acts of translation in history — politically, linguistically, and religiously.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: ### The Erasmian Correction

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: The immediate trigger: Erasmus published a new critical edition of the Greek New Testament (1516), correcting the Vulgate and restoring original Greek. This demonstrated that Jerome's Latin had translation errors with theological consequences.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: The metanoeite/paenitentiam agite example: Erasmus showed that the Greek word means "repent" (change your inner disposition) not "do penance" (perform sacramental acts). Luther's 95 Theses begin from this insight.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: ### Luther's Translation Method

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: Luther's famous statement from the *Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen* (Letter on Translation, 1530):

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: > "I must ask the mother in the house, the children in the street, the common man in the marketplace, and listen to what they say and translate accordingly, so that they can understand and see that one is speaking to them in German."

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther
History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
1. VERNACULAR NATURALIZATION:
     Use the German that common people actually speak.
     Not Latinate theological German but market German,
     kitchen German, children's German.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
2. SENSE-FOR-SENSE (Ciceronian):
     "In the German tongue one must not ask the Latin
     letters how to speak German... one must ask the
     mother at home, the children on the street,
     the common man in the market."

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
3. THEOLOGICAL COMMITMENTS EMBEDDED:
     Controversial addition: "alone" to Romans 3:28
     "A man is justified by faith [alone], apart from works"
     Greek has no "alone" (monon)
     Latin has no "alone"
     Luther: "alone" is grammatically natural in German;
     also theologically necessary (sola fide)
     Catholic critics: he added a word to scripture!
     Luther: the sense demands it

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
4. LINGUISTIC STANDARDIZATION:
     Luther chose East Middle German (the dialect
     of the Saxon Chancery) as his base.
     Because his Bible was read throughout Germany,
     this dialect became the basis of standard German
     (Hochdeutsch). Luther's Bible is to German
     what the KJV is to English — the linguistic
     standard-setter.
```

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: ### Political Consequences

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: The Protestant Reformation spread faster because the Bible was in German and could be printed. Gutenberg's press (1450s) made mass distribution possible. Luther's German Bible was a bestseller — ~200,000 copies sold between 1534 and 1574. Common people could now read scripture and evaluate priests' claims against the text.

sections.text: ## 18th-19th Century: Domestication Dominant

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: The 18th century was the era of classical domestication. Pope's Homer is the paradigm:

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: **Alexander Pope's *Iliad* (1715-1720)**: Pope did not know Greek (he used cribs). He produced a celebrated English poem in heroic couplets that reads magnificently as 18th-century English verse. Homer "speaks" in Augustan English.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: Matthew Arnold's criticism: Pope's Homer has nothing of the "plainness and directness" or "rapid fire" of the original. It is a great poem but not a translation of Homer; it is Pope.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther
History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
"TRANSLATORS" WHO BARELY KNEW THE SOURCE LANGUAGE:
  • Fitzgerald's Omar Khayyam (Rubaiyat, 1859):
    Fitzgerald had modest Persian; produced beloved
    English poem. "A Pot of Wine, a Loaf of Bread--
    and Thou." Persian original: harder-edged,
    more ambiguous.

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
"FAITHFUL" TRANSLATORS WHO KNEW THE LANGUAGE:
  • Constance Garnett (1861-1946):
    Translated almost all of Russian literature
    (Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Chekhov, Turgenev)
    into English 1890-1920s.
    Made Russian literature accessible to English readers.
    Criticized by Nabokov for over-domesticating,
    normalizing Russian syntax into English smoothness,
    losing the "Russian-ness."
    Counter: Without Garnett, English-speakers would
    have no Dostoevsky at all. Good enough translation
    that opens a literature is better than no translation.
```

sections.text: ## 20th Century: Translation Theory Becomes Academic

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: The 20th century saw translation theory professionalized:

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
- **Nida** (1964): Linguistic-based equivalence theory (see 01-EQUIVALENCE-PROBLEM)
- **Polysystem theory** (Even-Zohar, 1978): Translated literature occupies a position in the target culture's literary system. When a culture's literature is "young" or "peripheral," translations are central (Hebrew literature in the early 20th century, when translated classics shaped the emerging Hebrew literary tradition). When literature is "established," translations are peripheral.
- **Descriptive Translation Studies** (Toury, 1980s): Describe what translators actually do (norms), not what they should do (rules). Translation norms include initial norm (source-orientation vs. target-orientation) and operational norms (specific choices made).
- **Skopos theory** (Vermeer, 1984): Translation is determined by its *Skopos* (purpose). A legal contract needs a different translation than a novel. The Skopos, not faithfulness to the original, determines the appropriate translation strategy.

sections.text: ## Localization Industry (1980s-present)

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text: Localization (*l10n* — L + 10 letters + N; the learner will recognize this as the standard abbreviation pattern) is the industrialization of translation for software, product, and content:

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
SOURCE TEXT
  (English master)
       │
       ▼
  TRANSLATION MEMORY (TM)
  Previous translations stored; new text matched against TM
  100% match: reuse previous translation (no cost)
  Fuzzy match: edit existing translation
  New text: human translation + MT post-editing
       │
       ▼
  GLOSSARY / TERM MANAGEMENT
  Ensure consistent terminology across products
  ("click," "tap," "select" consistently translated
   to same terms)
       │
       ▼
  LOCALIZATION TESTING
  UI strings fit in their containers?
  Date/number formats correct?
  Right-to-left text (Arabic, Hebrew) rendering?
  Cultural appropriateness review?
       │
       ▼
  LOCALIZED PRODUCT
  (in up to 100+ languages for major tech products)

sections.text: ## Decision Cheat Sheet

metadata.title: History of Translation: Cicero to Jerome to Luther

sections.text:
| Period | Key figure | Method | Lasting contribution |
|--------|-----------|--------|---------------------|
| 46 BCE | Cicero | Sense-for-sense | Established the basic debate |
| 382 CE | Jerome | Sense-for-sense (except scripture) | Vulgate; word-for-word reverence for scripture |
| 12th c. | Gerard of Cremona | Literal (Arabic → Latin) | Greek science returned to Europe |
| 1522 | Luther | Dynamic vernacular | German standard language; Reformation enabled |
| 1715 | Pope | Domestication | English literary translation tradition |
| 1890s | Garnett | Fluent domestication | Russian literature in English |
| 1978 | Even-Zohar | Polysystem (descriptive) | Translation in its cultural context |
